title: Inquest report calls for better cell inspections
article: An inquest report released Tuesday offers recommendations on how the province and federal government might improve a woefully inadequate jail and policing system in the turbulent community of Pauingassi First Nation after the October 2005 cell death of 23-year-old Darlene Rose Owens.
The report by provincial judge Janice leMaistre calls for better cell inspections and more medical training for law enforcement officials in Pauingassi.

On Oct. 19, 2005, a band constable with no medical training and no formal police training took the intoxicated young woman to an RCMP cell to sober her up after a disturbance. There, a jail guard with no basic medical training was in charge of overseeing Owens, who, less than three hours later, hung herself from a cell door using her shirt.

The inquest report calls on the province to negotiate with the federal government to create a recruiting program to find more qualified jail guards in the remote fly-in community about 280 kilometres northeast of Winnipeg.
It also points the finger at both levels of government to improve First Nations policing across Manitoba, including more work on recruitment and training of officers who work in those communities.

"It is unclear whether CPR properly administered could have saved (Darlene) Owens. However, all band constables, night patrols, guards and other persons responsible for prisoner safety should have regular first aid and CPR training to ensure they are equipped to provide basic emergency care when required," said the report, which notes law enforcement officials in the community now receive first aid and CPR training before working.
The report states before Owens' hanging death, the RCMP conducted a province-wide review of jail cells in August 2005 to study which ones met standards and which cells required safety improvements.

The cell door Owens hung herself on had a loose door knob, according to inquest testimony. An RCMP official told the inquest after Owens death the RCMP found about 30 cells across Manitoba with locks designed similar to the one in the cell where the young woman died.
Most of those cells have had their doors replaced with sliding doors without knobs, said the inquest report.
An RCMP official who replaced the lock said cells are not regularly inspected, according to the inquest report.
The report then recommends the province start negotiations with the federal government and First Nations for regular inspections of RCMP cells.
The province's Justice Department and RCMP D Division said Tuesday they could not comment on the report.
